name: Dodge / Avoid
subtitle: Survive under continuous pressure and spatial constraints; the core revolves around hit detection, windows, and rhythm.
demoRuleHint: Rule: Hazard generation → Warning/trajectory → Player movement → Hit detection (hit/near miss) → Feedback (damage/Invincibility frames)
problemsSolved: Make failure reasons attributable (why you were hit, where safety lies)
Turn near misses into satisfying moments rather than just staying alive
Control intensity with a pressure curve (density/velocity/rhythm) to avoid pure numeric stacking
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the minimal survival loop — spawn → telegraph → move → judge → feedback — and reproduce one graze judgment in the demo
Intermediate: write the full hit-judgment contract (hitbox, graze zone, invincibility frames, respawn protection) and tune forgiveness parameters that keep beginners from churning
Advanced: design the pressure curve (density × speed × time ramp structure) and verify difficulty health with graze rate and survival-time distribution
minimalRules: Movement: Player movement and constraints (speed, turning, boundaries)
Hit detection: Hit radius and resolution (damage/failure/Invincibility frames)
systemLoopHint: Input (movement/dodging) → Prediction (read warning) → Hit detection (hit/near miss) → Feedback (damage/survival) → Pressure change → New input

combos.effect: Output while evading, creating a 'positioning and shooting' loop
Convert survival time/perfect dodges into progression resources
Randomize hazard patterns, emphasizing adaptation and reading the map

advancedWarnings: Unclear warnings make failures unaccountable (players feel unjustified)
Too fast speed with weak feedback turns the experience into 'passively getting hit'
Overly strict hit detection compresses expressive space; overly lenient loses tension
advancedAlgoRefs: Generation: Bullet/obstacle generator and difficulty curve
Hit detection: Circle/capsule collision, near-miss detection, invincibility frame window

demoLab.title: Hit Tolerance Experiment
demoLab.action: Drag "Forgiveness Window (hitbox shrink, px)" from 0 up to 24, then deliberately let bullets graze past your ship
demoLab.observe: Tolerance = the hitbox is one ring smaller than the visuals: at 0px a graze kills, at 24px players dare to thread between bullets. The gap between the two circles is your near-miss budget — too strict crushes showmanship, too loose kills the tension

demoLab.title: Near-Miss Reward Experiment
demoLab.action: Pull "Graze Bonus" from 0 to 50, then set "Bullet Density" to 3+ and actively fly close to bullets
demoLab.observe: A graze bonus turns dodging from survival into a chased thrill: hazards become score resources. The higher the reward, the closer players hug danger — one parameter rewrites the whole risk-reward curve

demoLab.title: Density Pressure Curve
demoLab.action: Step "Bullet Density" from 1 up to 5, surviving 20 seconds at each level
demoLab.observe: Density is the pressure-curve knob: each +1 visibly shrinks the safe space ratio. Density alone is not difficulty — real difficulty is density × tolerance: dense + forgiving stays casual, sparse + strict still kills

intro.what: Hazards keep flying at you and your job is to stay alive — bullet-hell shooters, Flappy Bird, and dodgeball-style games are all built on this.
intro.feel: You drag your character through a storm of bullets, weaving between them; the split second where one grazes past without killing you makes your heart skip — that "so close" thrill is the signature move.
intro.why: It is the purest sample of "difficulty as rhythm" — if you want to learn how to make players tense without feeling cheated, start here.

concept: Dodge play breaks "survival" into a chain of readable, moment-to-moment judgments: every hazard has a telegraph, a trajectory, and a hitbox, and every dodge immediately reports its outcome and its reason. The hard part is not the dodging — it is the credibility and forgiveness of the judgment: the gap between hitbox and visual circle is your thrill budget, and invincibility frames plus graze feedback decide whether a failure is learnable. The fairness players feel is built from these invisible judgment-engine details.
designNotes: Thrill is a designed resource: how many pixels the hitbox sits inside the visual circle is exactly how brave players dare to be — too strict and they turtle up, too loose and the tension is gone. That gap is worth tuning more than bullet speed.

"Nearly died" beats "perfectly dodged": graze bonuses turn threats into resources, luring players toward danger — counterintuitively, rewarding grazes makes players safer, because they start studying trajectories on purpose.

Only attributable failure earns a retry: with unclear telegraphs, players feel "wronged" instead of "I messed up" — telegraph lead time is not an accessibility feature; it is the fairness foundation of dodge play.

value.player: Dodging feeds a safe craving for danger — a bullet grazing past without killing you gets converted by the brain into pure thrill. Forgiveness windows and graze bonuses mass-produce that moment, letting players harvest small wins swinging between "I almost died" and "I can’t believe I didn’t."
value.ecosystem: Bullet-dodging is one of the lowest-barrier forms in action gaming: one finger, ten seconds a run, naturally suited to fragmented time and short-video sharing.
value.transfer: Learn dodge play and you learn pressure-curve and forgiveness engineering — density ramps, hitbox scaling, telegraph lead time — knobs you will keep turning in runners, shooters, and boss fights.
